name: Self-propaganda
statement: Self-propaganda is the name given to talking oneself into a belief and then refusing the evidence against it, and no effect is measured under that name.
meaning: The label describes an outcome and names other people's mechanisms to explain it. Its Wikipedia article attributes the process to confirmation bias and cognitive dissonance, then gives four examples: filter bubbles, confirmation bias again, communal reinforcement and echo chambers. Each of those has a research literature. Two have entries here, confirmation bias at entry 5 and cognitive dissonance at entry 24. What the label adds is a heading. It states no prediction that distinguishes it from selective exposure, from dissonance reduction, or from self-persuasion, entry 297, which is the studied case of a person moving their own attitude by producing the argument for it. A term that can only be tested by testing something else is a summary rather than a claim, and the measurements below belong to the things it summarises.

origin.who: an anonymous Wikipedia editor writing as Slokunshialgo
origin.note: No coining publication was located in the indexes searched, and 2006 is the date the label entered Wikipedia rather than a proven first use. Wikipedia cites a 1997 cognitive therapy volume at the page where the phrase would sit, and Google Books would not show that page, so an earlier print use is neither confirmed nor ruled out. The first revision of the Wikipedia article, timestamped 7 March 2006, carried no citations and was tagged as a psychology stub. It defined the term as ordinary propaganda "done to oneself" and said the person "will go over every aspect of their side of the 'argument'" and "refuse to look at any alternatives". The article has carried a "more citations needed" banner dated May 2010 since then. It sits in Wikipedia's Category:Cognitive biases, and the word does not appear in Wikipedia's own List of cognitive biases.

evidence: Nothing below is a measurement of self-propaganda, because there is none. The article carries ten citations. Two are Google Books links, to a cognitive therapy volume and to a book on propaganda in the helping professions, and a third is a Skeptic's Dictionary entry. Then come a political theory piece reachable only through a university proxy, a doctoral thesis, a dead CiteSeerX link and a peer-reviewed article on memory for personality feedback. The last three are a newspaper opinion column and two magazine pieces. Not one is a study of self-propaganda, and none was obtained for this entry. What has been measured is selective exposure, the preference for information that agrees with one's existing position. Hart, Albarracin, Eagly, Brechan, Lindberg and Merrill collected 67 eligible reports containing 91 studies, which supplied 300 statistically independent groups and just under 8,000 participants. The average effect was d = 0.36, 95% CI [0.34, 0.39] by fixed-effects analysis and d = 0.38, 95% CI [0.32, 0.44] by random effects, with an unweighted mean of 0.38. Effect sizes were heterogeneous. The preference weakened where participants' views had been supported before they chose, where those views were not tied to their values or held with conviction, where the available information was of low quality, and where their confidence was high. It reversed into a preference for disagreeable information when that information helped accomplish a current goal. Their paper opens by noting that diverse information in an environment does not guarantee that a person's views will be equally diverse.

examples.text: Someone leaning towards a purchase spends an evening assembling reasons for it and looks for none against. He ends more certain than the evidence he gathered would carry, and the argument that convinced him was his own.

A reader follows the accounts that say what he already thinks and reads the resulting agreement as independent support. Nothing in that is separable from selective exposure and communal reinforcement, which each have a name and a literature of their own.
A man goes over his side of a dispute until every objection has an answer waiting. By the time the other person speaks, whatever they offer arrives at a position built in order to refuse it.

replication.headline: No study of self-propaganda was found, because nothing is operationalised under the name. Its components are measured, and two of those measurements cut against the popular account.
replication.detail: Crossref returns no work carrying the term in its title, searched on 21 September 2026. Europe PMC finds the phrase in eight documents that day, none of them a study of it, and the only title match is a patent for an egg with a self-propaganda function. Two adjacent results contradict the label as written. Wikipedia calls self-propaganda a form of self-deception; Zhang and Rand ran two preregistered experiments, at 1,609 and 2,399 participants, comparing an incentivised persuasion task with an incentivised summary task, found the same amount of belief shift in both, and report that completing the summary task first cut the later shift roughly fivefold. Their conclusion is that the shift comes from exposure to goal-aligned arguments rather than from a motive to deceive oneself. Wikipedia also offers the Facebook filter bubble as a case. Nyhan and 29 colleagues measured that the median US Facebook user in 2020 saw 50.4% of their content from like-minded sources against 14.7% from cross-cutting ones, then ran a field experiment on 23,377 consenting users. Between 24 September and 23 December 2020 the intervention pushed like-minded exposure down to 36.2% in the treatment group while the control group held at 53.7%. Eight preregistered attitudinal measures, among them affective polarisation, ideological extremity and belief in false claims, did not move.

limits: The search covered Crossref by bibliographic and title query, Europe PMC, PubMed and general web search, all on 21 September 2026. OpenAlex refused again, reporting that the free daily budget shared by this network's address was spent. Semantic Scholar's search endpoint answered every attempt with a rate limit that day, so its earlier null result was not re-checked. No psychology-specific database such as PsycINFO was searched, and Google Books was not searched systematically. Absence of a study is a statement about those places. The ten references on the Wikipedia article were not obtained: two are Google Books previews, one needs a university proxy, one is a doctoral thesis and one link is a CiteSeerX downloads-exceeded page. Zhang and Rand carries a CC BY licence at Elsevier, yet ScienceDirect answered with a 403 on every attempt that day, across three user agents and across the article page, the PDF route and the reader host. That is a block on the fetcher rather than a paywall. No copy sits elsewhere: OpenAlex, Unpaywall and Semantic Scholar each list the publisher alone, PubMed Central holds no deposit, and SSRN refused the earlier working paper. The paper was read in abstract at Europe PMC, so the fivefold figure is the authors' own summary of Study 2 and the two tasks are described from the abstract. DiFonzo and colleagues' 2013 paper is closed at the publisher, and the one repository copy, a submitted version at the Australian National University, is embargoed until 31 December 2037 behind a request-a-copy form. That is not a paywall either, and the paper is named on this page without being read. Hart and colleagues were read in full from the author manuscript at PMC, which is not the published typesetting, and Nyhan and colleagues in full at Nature. Neither study was designed to test self-propaganda, and both are cited here for the components the label borrows rather than as verdicts on it.
misreadings: The first misreading is that the term marks a distinct finding. It marks a folder. Its own page explains it by confirmation bias, cognitive dissonance and communal reinforcement, which is a list of other topics rather than a mechanism. The second is that it is self-deception under another name. Zhang and Rand's preregistered studies locate the effect in what arguments a person is exposed to, and an incentive to persuade was not needed to produce it. The third is that echo chambers demonstrate it. Cutting like-minded content by about a third for three months changed what 23,377 Facebook users saw and left all eight preregistered attitude measures where they were. The fourth concerns the one named psychologist on the page. Wikipedia's claim that Nicholas DiFonzo found partisans polarising when segregated and less so when mixed is sourced to a 2011 New York Times opinion column. A peer-reviewed paper by DiFonzo and seven colleagues on rumour clustering and polarisation exists in the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, and it is not the citation the page gives. The fifth is that selective exposure is unconditional. Hart and colleagues found the preference reversing where uncongenial information served a goal the person had.

sources.text: Wikipedia, Self-propaganda. The article that carries the term as a cognitive bias. Used to find the claims examined above and quoted as their carrier, not relied on for any finding.

Wikipedia, Self-propaganda, revision 42566519 of 7 March 2006 by Slokunshialgo. The first version of the article, read as raw wikitext. Source for the 2006 date and the wording quoted in the origin note.
Wikipedia, List of cognitive biases. Searched as raw wikitext for the term, which does not appear.

Hart, W., Albarracin, D., Eagly, A. H., Brechan, I., Lindberg, M. J., & Merrill, L. (2009). Feeling validated versus being correct: A meta-analysis of selective exposure to information. Psychological Bulletin, 135(4), 555-588. Read in full from the author manuscript at PMC4797953. Source for every selective-exposure figure above.

Nyhan, B., Settle, J., Thorson, E., Wojcieszak, M., Barbera, P., Chen, A. Y., et al. (2023). Like-minded sources on Facebook are prevalent but not polarizing. Nature, 620(7972), 137-144. Open access, read in full. Source for the exposure percentages and the null result on eight preregistered measures.

Zhang, Y., & Rand, D. G. (2025). Self-persuasion does not imply self-deception. Cognition, 263, 106215. Read in abstract at Europe PMC on 21 September 2026. The full text is CC BY at Elsevier but ScienceDirect returned 403 to every request, and no repository, PubMed Central or SSRN copy was served.

Named because Wikipedia's DiFonzo claim cites a newspaper column instead. Closed at the publisher, and the Australian National University holds a submitted version embargoed to 31 December 2037 behind a request-a-copy form.
